questions.prompt: Two house-price models have the same MAE, but model B has a much higher RMSE. What does that tell you about model B?
options: Its errors are mostly small, with a few very large misses
It is biased upward on every single prediction
It explains less variance, so its R^2 must be negative
Its errors are all roughly the same moderate size
questions.explanation: RMSE squares residuals before averaging, so a gap between RMSE and MAE signals a few large errors. Equal-sized errors would make RMSE equal MAE.

questions.prompt: A demand forecaster reports MAPE across thousands of products, many of which sell 0 or 1 units on most days. What is the main problem?
options: MAPE ignores the sign of the errors entirely
MAPE cannot be computed with more than one product
Dividing by tiny or zero actuals makes MAPE explode or break
MAPE is always smaller than MAE, hiding the error
questions.explanation: MAPE divides each error by the actual value, so near-zero sales produce huge or undefined percentages. WAPE (sum of absolute errors over sum of actuals) avoids this.

questions.prompt: Your model's residual-vs-prediction plot shows a funnel: residuals spread wider as predictions grow. What is a sensible next step?
options: Add more trees, since the funnel means underfitting
Model a log-transformed target or use a scale-aware loss
Switch the reported metric from RMSE to R^2
Remove the largest predictions from the test set
questions.explanation: A funnel means error variance grows with the target (heteroscedasticity). A log target or relative-error loss stabilizes it; changing the reported metric does not fix the model.

questions.prompt: Two search systems both have recall@10 = 0.8. System A usually puts the right answer at rank 1; system B at rank 8. Which metric separates them?
options: Recall@10, computed with more queries
Hit rate@10 averaged over all queries
Precision@10 on the same set of queries
MRR, which rewards relevant items ranked early
questions.explanation: Recall, precision and hit rate at k ignore order inside the top k. MRR uses 1/rank of the first relevant item, so rank 1 scores 1.0 and rank 8 scores 0.125.

questions.prompt: Your relevance labels are graded 0 (bad) to 3 (perfect), and users mostly look at the first few results. Which metric fits best?
options: NDCG@k, which uses graded gains and discounts lower ranks
Hit rate@k, which only checks for any relevant item
Recall@k, which counts all relevant items equally
Accuracy of a relevant/irrelevant classifier
questions.explanation: NDCG handles graded relevance and discounts by position, then normalizes by the ideal ordering so scores are comparable across queries.

questions.prompt: A RAG chatbot gives wrong answers. You find the gold passage is in the retrieved top 5 for only 40% of questions. What should you fix first?
options: The LLM's prompt, so it reasons more carefully
The answer grader, which is probably too strict
The retriever, since the evidence rarely reaches the context
The output length limit, which truncates answers
questions.explanation: Recall@5 of 0.4 means the generator usually never sees the evidence, so no prompt change can fix most errors. Evaluate and improve retrieval separately from generation.

questions.prompt: Among all predictions your model makes with 0.9 confidence, only 70% are correct. How should you describe it?
options: Underconfident; its scores should be pushed up
Overconfident; its confidence exceeds its accuracy
Well calibrated, since 70% is above chance
Poorly discriminating; its AUROC must be near 0.5
questions.explanation: Calibration compares stated confidence to observed accuracy. Saying 0.9 while being right 70% of the time is overconfidence; it says nothing directly about ranking quality.

questions.prompt: You must calibrate a 10-class image model without changing which class it predicts. Which method guarantees that?
options: Isotonic regression fitted separately per class
Retraining with focal loss and gamma = 2
Oversampling rare classes in the training data
Temperature scaling of the logits on a held-out set
questions.explanation: Dividing all logits by one temperature T preserves their order, so the argmax and accuracy stay the same. Per-class isotonic fits can change the top class.

questions.prompt: After Platt scaling, a fraud model's ECE drops from 0.12 to 0.02. What happens to its AUROC?
options: It stays the same, because the mapping is monotone
It rises, because calibrated scores rank better
It falls, because calibration trades off with ranking
It becomes undefined until the threshold is retuned
questions.explanation: Platt scaling is an increasing function of the score, so the ordering of examples is unchanged and AUROC is identical. Calibration and discrimination are separate properties.

questions.prompt: A test of a new checkout page gives p = 0.03. Which statement is correct?
options: There is a 3% chance the new page has no effect
There is a 97% chance the new page is better
Data this extreme would occur 3% of the time if there were no effect
The new page improves conversion by about 3%
questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme assuming the null is true. It is not the probability the null is true, nor the effect size.

questions.prompt: A team checks its A/B dashboard every morning and stops the test the first day p dips below 0.05. What is the problem?
options: Daily checks reduce power, hiding real effects
Repeated peeking inflates the false-positive rate well above 5%
Stopping early makes the confidence interval too wide
The p-value cannot be computed before the test ends
questions.explanation: Each look is another chance for noise to cross the threshold; with 10 looks the false-positive rate reaches about 19%. Fix the sample size in advance or use a sequential test.

questions.prompt: You compare two classifiers on the same 2,000 test examples and want a confidence interval for the F1 difference. What is a sound approach?
options: Run each model once and report the raw F1 gap
Use a two-sample t-test on the two F1 scores
Evaluate each model on a different random half of the test set
Paired bootstrap: resample examples, recompute both F1s, take percentiles
questions.explanation: Resampling the same examples for both models keeps the comparison paired and works for any metric. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the differences give a 95% interval.

questions.prompt: Delivery times are usually 30 minutes, but a few orders take 5 hours due to logging errors. You want a typical-time prediction. Which loss fits?
options: MSE, because it is the most common loss
MAE or Huber, because they limit the outliers' pull
Squared log error, because it is always unbiased
Cross-entropy, because times are positive
questions.explanation: MSE predicts the mean, which bad 5-hour records drag upward. MAE targets the median and Huber caps each outlier's gradient at delta.

questions.prompt: A warehouse wants a stock forecast that is enough 95% of the time, because running out is far worse than overstocking. Which loss?
options: Quantile (pinball) loss with q = 0.95
Huber loss with a large delta
MSE with targets multiplied by 0.95
MAE on standardized targets
questions.explanation: Pinball loss with q = 0.95 charges under-prediction 19x more than over-prediction, so the model learns the 95th percentile of demand.

questions.prompt: You rescale targets from dollars to thousands of dollars but keep Huber delta = 1.0. What changes?
options: Nothing, because Huber loss is scale-invariant
The model now ignores all outliers completely
Huber becomes equivalent to cross-entropy
Delta now means $1,000, so far fewer errors count as outliers
questions.explanation: Delta is measured in target units. After rescaling, delta = 1 corresponds to $1,000, so the loss stays quadratic for much larger errors; retune delta after rescaling.

questions.prompt: Your PyTorch model ends with a softmax layer and you train it with nn.CrossEntropyLoss. Training is sluggish. Why?
options: CrossEntropyLoss needs one-hot labels, not class indices
Softmax outputs are too large for the loss to handle
CrossEntropyLoss applies log-softmax itself, so softmax runs twice
Cross-entropy only works for binary classification
questions.explanation: nn.CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits and applies log-softmax internally. Feeding it probabilities squashes the scores twice and weakens gradients.

questions.prompt: An object detector sees 100,000 easy background boxes for every few real objects, and the easy boxes dominate the loss. What helps most directly?
options: Hinge loss, so probabilities become calibrated
Focal loss, which down-weights well-classified examples
Label smoothing with eps = 0.5 on all classes
Removing the sigmoid and using MSE on logits
questions.explanation: Focal loss multiplies cross-entropy by (1 - p_t)^gamma, shrinking the loss of easy examples (100x at p_t = 0.9 with gamma = 2) so hard ones drive learning.

questions.prompt: A binary model computes torch.log(torch.sigmoid(z)) and gets NaN losses when logits reach -800. What is the fix?
options: Use binary_cross_entropy_with_logits on the raw logits
Lower the learning rate until the logits stay small
Replace the sigmoid with a softmax over one class
Add class weights so negatives count less
questions.explanation: sigmoid(-800) underflows to 0 and log(0) is -inf. The fused loss uses the stable form max(z, 0) - z*y + log(1 + exp(-|z|)), which never takes log of 0.

questions.prompt: A triplet has d(anchor, positive) = 0.3 and d(anchor, negative) = 1.2 with margin 0.5. What is its loss, and why does that matter?
options: 0.4, so it pushes the negative slightly farther
1.4, so it is a hard triplet worth mining
0.9, the gap between the two distances
0, so it contributes no gradient and wastes compute
questions.explanation: max(0, 0.3 - 1.2 + 0.5) = 0. Easy triplets already satisfy the margin, which is why hard or semi-hard negative mining is used.

questions.prompt: You train a CLIP-style model with InfoNCE but must cut the batch size from 4,096 to 64. What is the main risk?
options: Each example gets far fewer in-batch negatives, weakening the signal
The similarity matrix stops being square
Temperature can no longer be learned
The loss changes from cross-entropy to MSE
questions.explanation: With in-batch negatives each row has N - 1 negatives, so a smaller batch means an easier task and weaker gradients. Memory banks or mined hard negatives can compensate.

questions.prompt: For a recommender you only know which items each user clicked, not ratings. You want clicked items ranked above unclicked ones. Which loss fits?
options: MSE on a predicted star rating
Triplet loss with a margin of zero
BPR: -log sigmoid(s_clicked - s_unclicked)
Hinge loss on the absolute click count
questions.explanation: BPR is a pairwise ranking loss built for implicit feedback: it only cares that the clicked item scores higher than a sampled unclicked one.

questions.prompt: Model A reports perplexity 12 and model B reports 18 on the same text, but they use different tokenizers. What can you conclude?
options: A is better, because lower perplexity always wins
B is better, because larger vocabularies raise perplexity
They are tied once you take the square root
Nothing yet; compare bits per byte or character instead
questions.explanation: Perplexity is per token, and token sizes differ between tokenizers. A tokenizer-independent unit such as bits per byte makes the comparison fair.

questions.prompt: You fit a single Gaussian Q to a two-peaked distribution P by minimizing reverse KL(Q || P). What do you expect?
options: Q spreads wide to cover both peaks
Q locks onto one peak and ignores the other
Q matches P exactly, since KL is symmetric
Q collapses to a point mass between the peaks
questions.explanation: Reverse KL heavily penalizes Q putting mass where P has little, so Q is mode-seeking and settles on one peak. Forward KL(P || Q) would spread Q over both.

questions.prompt: A VAE's KL term drops to nearly 0 and its samples look the same no matter which z you feed in. What has happened?
options: Mode collapse caused by the discriminator
The ELBO has become an exact likelihood
Posterior collapse: the decoder ignores the latent code
The noise schedule of the diffusion process is too short
questions.explanation: When the decoder is powerful enough to model data alone, q(z|x) matches the prior, the KL term vanishes and z carries no information. KL annealing or weaker decoders help.
